name: David Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi David, thanks for doing this. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Brightfold, a small agency of eight people in an old warehouse by the railway, and I mostly do packaging and labels for local food and drink makers. So one week it's cans for a craft brewery, the next it's jam labels for a farm shop, and I love that I can walk into a supermarket and pick up something I made. Mornings are usually client calls and sketching, afternoons are artwork and getting files ready for the printer. The worst part is the printer ringing at five to say a barcode is in the wrong spot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do AI tools fit into that, if at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. I'll use an image tool to rough up a mockup of a can on a shelf so a client can picture it, but I don't trust it for final art. I live with my partner Jonas, who teaches at a primary school, and we've got about three months of savings, which we're slowly building toward a deposit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a handy shortcut and not much more. Online I'd probably make a joke about all the people who quit their jobs to become prompt engineers. At work I'd just say the mockup tool saves me an hour a week and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty happy. Our clients like having a real person who visits the brewery and tastes the beer, and that doesn't go away. The only worry would be the usual one, that a big client like the dairy co-op takes their packaging in-house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep using the mockup tool when it helps. I'd keep putting two hundred a month toward the house deposit with Jonas. And I'd probably finally ask for a raise, because if nothing radical changes, I'm due one after three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. It feels like the version where I get to plan normal things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the dairy co-op. How much of Brightfold's work is that one client?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a fifth of the year, which is a lot for eight people. If they left, it wouldn't be because of AI, it'd be because they hired their own designer. I'd still be okay, I think, because I do most of the brewery work and those guys aren't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Jonas do with a normal few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy a small place, probably out past the ring road where it's cheaper. Get a dog, finally. Jonas wants a garden and I want a spare room I can turn into a little studio.

say: I'd say AI is a **handy shortcut** and not much more.
I'd mention the mockup tool saves me **an hour a week** and leave it there.
think: Clients still want a **real person** who visits the brewery and tastes the beer.
The only worry is a big client taking packaging **in-house**, which has nothing to do with AI.
do: Keep using the **mockup tool** when it saves time on client pitches.
Put **two hundred a month** toward the house deposit with my partner.
Ask for a **raise** after three years at the agency.
feel: **Calm**, because this is the version where I get to **plan normal things**.
S0.quote: Our clients like having a real person who visits the brewery and tastes the beer, and that doesn't go away.
fieldNote: His sense of safety comes from **client relationships**, not from any skill he guards.
He separates AI from the real risk, which is a big client going **in-house**.
Home plans are concrete: a **deposit**, a dog and a spare-room studio.

steps.text: Keep using the mockup tool for client pitches
Save two hundred a month toward a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to talk about who gets the time AI saves, the workers or the owners. I'd probably share stuff from the designers' union about fair use of these tools. At work I'd say let's get ahead of it together rather than pretend it isn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, half my job is on that list. Writing the little bits of label copy, checking the barcodes and allergen text, planning the print run, answering client emails, all of it. I think Brightfold won't sack anyone at first, but they won't replace Hannah when she goes on maternity leave, and the rest of us will be expected to do more with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down this winter and actually learn the packaging tools properly, the ones that check dielines and allergen text. I'd join the union, because if targets go up I want someone in my corner. I'd also stop the deposit savings for a year and keep that money as a buffer instead, which Jonas would hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into nervous. I like this job, and I can feel it getting thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pause the deposit. How did that conversation with Jonas go in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great. He'd say the house is the one stable thing we're working toward, and I'd say it's no good having a mortgage if my pay drops. We'd probably settle on half, a hundred a month to each pot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You also said the job feels thinner. What part would you miss most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sketching on site. Sitting in the brewery with a notebook while the head brewer tells me why the beer's called what it's called. If I end up just checking what a tool spits out, I'll have lost the bit I actually got into this for.

say: I'd ask **who gets the time** AI saves, the workers or the owners.
I'd share the **designers' union** guidance on fair use of these tools.
think: **Half my job** is on that list: label copy, checks, print planning and client emails.
My agency won't sack anyone at first, but it **won't replace** people who leave.
do: Learn the **packaging check tools** properly this winter.
Join the **designers' union** in case targets go up.
Split savings so **half** goes to a **buffer** instead of the house deposit.
feel: **Nervous**, because I like this job and can feel it **getting thinner**.
S1.quote: If I end up just checking what a tool spits out, I'll have lost the bit I actually got into this for.
fieldNote: He names his own tasks precisely and sees **half** of them on the card.
He expects attrition, not sackings: a colleague on leave **not replaced**.
The **deposit versus buffer** tension with his partner shows the money pressure is real.

steps.text: Learn the dieline and allergen-checking tools this winter
Join the designers' union in case targets rise
Move half the deposit savings into an emergency buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we needed rules years ago, and we'd better get them now. I'd be pushing for some kind of basic income, because there's no way the market sorts this out in two years. At work I'd try to get everyone talking to the owners together, not one by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone by 2029. Packaging design is thinking work with a printer at the end, and AI does the thinking part. The only bits left would be the press checks and the physical samples, and robots come for those three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd stop the deposit completely and build savings as fast as I can. I'd look at moving across to the print side, standing at the press and checking colour, because that's hands-on and buys a few years. Once it arrives I'd join every campaign for income support, and probably lean on Jonas's pay while I work out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Like the ground shifted and nobody warned us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Jonas's job feel any safer than yours here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching is safer for a while, I think, because someone still has to be in the room with thirty seven-year-olds. But marking and lesson planning are thinking work too. So we'd go from two incomes to one shaky one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the press buys a few years. Would you actually do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would, yes. I've stood next to the press at Carver Print plenty of times and I know the guys there. It's not what I trained for, but three years of wages while I figure things out is worth a lot.

say: I'd say we needed **rules years ago**, and we need them now.
I'd push for a **basic income**, because the market can't sort this out in two years.
think: My job is **gone by 2029**, because packaging design is thinking work.
The **press checks** last longer, but robots come for those three years later.
do: Stop the **house deposit** and build savings as fast as possible.
Move to the **print side** at Carver Print to check colour on the press.
Join campaigns for **income support** and lean on my partner's teaching pay.
feel: **Sick**, like the ground shifted and **nobody warned us**.
S2.quote: Packaging design is thinking work with a printer at the end, and AI does the thinking part.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** clearly and would move to the press to use it.
Both household incomes look **exposed**, though teaching less so at first.
His politics turn concrete: **basic income** and collective talks with the owners.

steps.text: Stop the house deposit and build cash savings instead
Ask Carver Print about a job checking colour on the press
Join campaigns for a basic income
Rely on his partner's teaching pay while he works out next steps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly, if governments actually start now. I'd be loud about retraining money for people in jobs like mine. At work I'd push the owners to tell us honestly what they're planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it gives me a career change instead of a crash. I'd be thirty-two when AGI hits, which is still early. I'd have time to train for something where people pay for a person, not just for the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI more at work for the next couple of years, because it's going to be expected and I'd rather keep my wage while it lasts. In the evenings I'd start looking seriously at teaching design at a college, or at becoming a print production manager, something with people and machines. I'd keep the deposit going but slower, a hundred a month instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can work with. Five years feels like a runway, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching design, if AI can do the design?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people will still want to make things with their hands and minds, even if they don't have to. Jonas loves teaching and he's good at it, and I've always liked the workshops I've run for the brewery's apprentices. I don't know if it pays, but it feels like work with a person in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Brightfold would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hannah, honestly. She's back from leave with a baby and she's the one doing all the copywriting, which goes first. I'd tell her to start looking now, while there's still time.

I'd be loud about **retraining money** for people in jobs like mine.
think: Five years gives me a **career change** instead of a crash.
At **thirty-two** I'd still be early enough to train for something new.
do: Use **AI tools** more at work to keep my wage while it lasts.
Look into **teaching design** at a college or print production management.
Slow the deposit to **a hundred a month** instead of two.
feel: **Worried**, but five years feels like a **runway**, not a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a runway, not a cliff.
fieldNote: More time turns his fear into a **plan**, which drops his mood to anxious.
He is drawn to **teaching**, partly because his partner models it daily.
He worries more about a **colleague** with a new baby than about himself.

steps.text: Use AI tools daily at Brightfold to keep his wage
Research college courses for teaching design
Cut the deposit savings to a hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, let's not waste it arguing whether it's real. I'd be pushing for the union to start training schemes right now. Online I'd probably be the annoying person posting long threads about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd get maybe eight good years of design work, which is more than most careers get anyway. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, and that's a scary age to start over but not impossible. The question is whether whatever I switch to is safe from the robots three years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and the house plan, and buy a small place in the next couple of years while I've still got a steady wage. I'd do a part-time teaching qualification over two or three years. I'd use the tools at work as they come, but I wouldn't go out of my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, with a knot in my stomach. Ten years is long enough that I could pretend it isn't coming, and I don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a house before your job ends sounds risky. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Jonas's job will likely last longer than mine, and a mortgage on one teaching wage is just about doable out past the ring road. Renting gets worse every year. I'd rather own something small than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a nineteen-year-old who wants to study design?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it if you love it. Learn to teach or to run a workshop alongside. Don't bet everything on making pictures for a living. That's hard to say, because it's what I did.

say: I'd call **ten years a gift** and push to start training schemes now.
I'd post **long threads** about it online, which would annoy people.
think: I'd get maybe **eight good years** of design work before it lands.
The real question is whether my **next job** is safe from robots three years later.
do: Buy a **small place** in the next couple of years while my wage is steady.
Do a part-time **teaching qualification** over two or three years.
Use **AI tools** at work as they arrive, without chasing them.
feel: **Mostly okay**, with a **knot** in my stomach.
S4.quote: Learn to teach or to run a workshop alongside. Don't bet everything on making pictures for a living.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets him keep **ordinary plans**, like buying a house, but he can't fully relax.
He bets on his **partner's job** lasting longer than his own.
His advice to young designers shows **regret** mixed with love for the trade.

steps.text: Buy a small place past the ring road while his wage is steady
Keep working at Brightfold and pick up tools as they arrive

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years and both our jobs change, and mine basically goes. What would help is money to live on while I retrain, and a union that's actually at the table when owners decide how to use these tools.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the clients. The farm shops and breweries I work for are tiny, and they'd be hit too. I don't want to be the guy who pushed a button that made every jam jar look the same.

headlineQuote: I don't want to be the guy who pushed a button that made every jam jar look the same.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old packaging designer** at an eight-person agency serving local breweries and farm shops.
He uses AI **now and then** for mockups and lives with his **partner**, a primary school teacher.
With about **three months saved**, he juggles a house deposit against a safety buffer.
He stays calm if AI stalls, but expects to **lose design work** in every AGI scenario.
His answers lean on the **union**, retraining money and a possible move into **teaching**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because both incomes change in two years and his job basically goes.
whatWouldHelp: A **union at the table** when owners decide how to use AI tools.
